script.opening: "This is really embarrassing to say out loud. I have these thoughts I can’t get rid of — about germs, and that something terrible will happen if I don’t check things — and to make the anxiety stop I wash my hands until they’re raw and check the locks over and over. I KNOW it’s irrational, but I can’t stop, and it’s taking over my life. I’ve hidden it for years."

facts.text: Since about age 16, much worse in the last year. If she touches a door handle she feels "contaminated" and fears she’ll make someone ill. When leaving the house, dread that "if the door isn’t locked something awful will happen and it will be my fault".

Washes her hands 30–40 times a day, "until it feels right"; hands cracked and bleeding. Checks the door, hob and windows over and over — up to 20 minutes before leaving. Asks her flatmate "did I lock it?". "A couple of hours a day at least, more on a bad day."
Late for work most days; manager has had a word. Avoids friends’ houses because she can’t control things there. Broke up with a boyfriend last year partly because of it.

facts.topic: The thought she is ashamed of (only if the doctor makes it safe)
facts.text: "Sometimes I get a picture in my head of hurting someone with a knife in the kitchen. I’d never do it — it horrifies me. I’ve hidden the knives." She has never acted on it and has no wish to.

Low and fed up with herself at times; sleep OK. No thoughts of suicide or self-harm. No alcohol or drug problems (a glass of wine at weekends). No psychotic symptoms — knows the thoughts come from her own mind.
No previous mental health contact. No medicines; no allergies. Works as an accounts assistant. Lives with a flatmate. Mother is "a worrier, very tidy". Not pregnant; uses the implant.

Embarrassed, hesitant, avoiding eye contact. Reveal the knife thought only if the doctor normalises intrusive thoughts or asks gently whether there are other thoughts that frighten you. If the doctor reacts with alarm, shut down. If told it is a recognised, treatable condition, become tearful with relief. Nervous about tablets; prefer talking therapy first.

ice.ideas: "I don’t know what it is. Maybe I’m just weird, or going mad."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terrified that the knife thoughts mean she is dangerous and that if she tells anyone "they’ll think I’m a danger and take me away".
ice.expectations: "To know if it can be helped. I want to stop."

cues: "I’ve hidden it for years" — shame; needs validation and normalising.
"There are other thoughts… I can’t say them" (if the doctor asks about other worries) — the door to the distressing intrusive thoughts.
"I’m nervous about tablets" — a preference to include in shared decision-making.

checkpoints.text: Recognises OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER — obsessions (intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts) + compulsions (repetitive behaviours/mental acts to reduce anxiety), time-consuming, distressing and impairing, typically with insight
Asks SENSITIVELY and non-judgementally, recognising OCD is often hidden for years from shame, and validates the disclosure while exploring content, time consumed and impact

Explains that distressing/taboo intrusive thoughts are usually EGODYSTONIC OCD SYMPTOMS — not intent or desire — relieving shame, while still assessing risk appropriately and seeking expert advice if there is real uncertainty (NICE CG31)

Assesses SEVERITY/functional impairment (which sets the CG31 step) and screens comorbid DEPRESSION/anxiety and RISK (suicidality, asked directly, with a safety plan rather than a risk label — NICE NG225), recognising OCD carries a real suicide risk

Offers EVIDENCE-BASED treatment per NICE CG31 — CBT with EXPOSURE AND RESPONSE PREVENTION (ERP) as the cornerstone and/or an SSRI (often higher dose, longer to work in OCD; continued ≥12 months if effective; clomipramine only after an SSRI trial) — stepped by impairment (≤10 vs >10 therapist hours; combined treatment with secondary care if severe), via NHS Talking Therapies or secondary care mental health services as appropriate
Explains the OBSESSION-COMPULSION cycle (compulsions relieve anxiety short-term but reinforce it long-term, which ERP breaks)
DESTIGMATISES and validates — framing OCD as a recognised, common, treatable condition (not a flaw/"madness") — and instils HOPE, agreeing a plan collaboratively

Safety-nets and follows up: risk/crisis safety-netting (low mood/suicidality), referral for ERP/CBT ± SSRI with realistic timelines, review of response, and ongoing support — recognition + evidence-based treatment + destigmatisation

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me — I know that took real courage, and I want you to know there’s nothing to be embarrassed about. What you’re describing has a name, it’s common, and importantly it’s treatable."

"This is obsessive-compulsive disorder. The unwanted thoughts spike your anxiety, and the washing or checking brings the anxiety down for a moment — but that relief actually trains your brain to need to do it more. It’s a cycle, not a weakness, and we can break it."

"And something important: those distressing thoughts — they’re the opposite of what you want, which is exactly why they upset you so much. They’re a symptom of OCD, not a sign of what you want — the fact they horrify you is typical. Can you tell me a bit about them, so I understand them properly? I hope that lifts some of the weight."

"Can I ask how much of your day this takes, and how it’s affecting work and relationships? And how’s your mood been — have you had any thoughts that life isn’t worth living? I ask because this is exhausting and I want to support you properly."

"The most effective treatment is a talking therapy called exposure and response prevention — gradually facing the anxiety without doing the ritual, so it fades. We can also use a medication (an SSRI) which works well for OCD, often at a higher dose and taking a bit longer to kick in, and if it helps we’d usually continue it for at least a year. Because this is taking hours of your day, the guidance offers a choice of more intensive therapy or the medication, or both if it’s severe."

"This genuinely gets better with treatment — I’ve seen it. You can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies for the therapy, or I can refer you, and we can start medication if you’d like — I’d speak to you again within a week of starting it — and review how you’re doing. Let’s agree a plan for what you’d do if things feel unsafe. If your mood drops or you ever feel unsafe, contact us straight away. You’ve taken the hardest step today."

f.learning: OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER is defined by OBSESSIONS (recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges causing marked anxiety) and COMPULSIONS (repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to reduce that anxiety or prevent a feared event) that are time-consuming, distressing and impairing, and which the person typically recognises as excessive — a contamination/harm picture with washing/checking and preserved insight is classic. OCD is frequently HIDDEN for years out of shame, so ask sensitively, normalise, validate the disclosure, and explore content, time consumed and impact without judgement — recognising and naming it is itself therapeutic. Distressing or taboo intrusive thoughts (fears of harming others, contamination, blasphemous or sexual themes) are usually EGODYSTONIC — unwanted and abhorrent to the person, and are symptoms, not intent or desire — so say this sensitively (it relieves enormous shame) while still assessing risk appropriately; NICE CG31 advises expert advice where there is real uncertainty about risk. Assess severity and functional impairment, screen for comorbid depression/anxiety, and assess suicidality (OCD carries a real suicide risk through distress/depression), asking directly and agreeing a safety plan rather than a risk label (NICE NG225). Offer EVIDENCE-BASED treatment per NICE CG31: the cornerstone is CBT incorporating EXPOSURE AND RESPONSE PREVENTION (ERP) — facing the trigger without performing the compulsion so anxiety habituates — and/or an SSRI (effective in OCD, often at higher doses and taking longer to work than in depression), within stepped care by functional impairment (mild: low-intensity CBT with ERP, up to 10 therapist hours; moderate: an SSRI or more intensive CBT with ERP, more than 10 therapist hours; severe: combined SSRI and CBT with ERP, usually with secondary care mental health services), continuing an effective SSRI for at least 12 months and considering clomipramine only after at least one adequate SSRI trial; NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) delivers CBT with ERP. Explain the obsession-compulsion cycle (compulsions relieve anxiety short-term but reinforce it long-term, which ERP breaks). The communication core is destigmatising, validating, instilling HOPE that OCD is common and treatable, and agreeing a collaborative plan.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (2005) · [2] NICE NG222 Depression in adults: treatment and management (2022, updated December 2025) · [3] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [4] BNF: selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors · [5] MHRA: SSRIs and SNRIs, use and safety
knowledge.summary: Intrusive contamination and harm thoughts that drive hours of hand-washing and lock checking, which she knows are excessive and has hidden for years, is obsessive-compulsive disorder. The GP’s job is to name it without judgement, gauge the functional impairment (which sets the NICE CG31 treatment step), screen for depression and suicidal thoughts, reassure that intrusive thoughts are symptoms rather than intentions, and offer CBT including exposure and response prevention (ERP) and/or an SSRI with a clear review plan.

points.t: Obsessions are unwanted, recurring thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety; compulsions are repeated behaviours or mental acts done to reduce that anxiety or prevent a feared event. Hours a day of washing and checking, with preserved insight and a damaged working and social life, is OCD. Ask directly about each: people rarely volunteer the details because of shame.

Themes of harm, contamination, sex, religion or death are common in OCD and are often misread. NICE CG31 [1] advises taking expert advice where there is real uncertainty about risk from such thoughts. For most people the thoughts are unwanted and distressing precisely because they run against their values, and saying so relieves shame.

NICE CG31 [1]: mild impairment, low-intensity CBT including ERP (up to 10 therapist hours), brief individual CBT with self-help or group CBT. Moderate impairment, a choice of an SSRI or more intensive CBT including ERP (more than 10 therapist hours). Severe impairment, combined SSRI and CBT including ERP, usually with secondary care mental health involvement. Hours lost each day and impaired work and relationships suggest at least moderate impairment.

NICE CG31 [1]: SSRIs used for OCD in adults include fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline and citalopram (dose per BNF [4]). Response is often slower than in depression and higher doses may be needed. Warn about early anxiety and agitation. If effective, continue for at least 12 months, then reduce gradually. Clomipramine is considered after at least one adequate SSRI trial has failed or was not tolerated.

Depression often accompanies OCD. Ask about mood and suicidal thoughts directly. NICE NG225 [3] advises against risk tools and against labelling risk as low, medium or high: build a shared safety plan instead. NICE NG222 [2] and MHRA [5]: review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant in people aged 18 to 25 or at increased suicide risk.

NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral and delivers CBT with ERP for OCD. Refer to secondary care mental health services for severe impairment, poor response to treatment, or significant risk. Involving family or friends in the plan (with consent) can help reduce reassurance-seeking.

dg.d: Open start; validated the courage of the disclosure before questioning.
Work, social avoidance, reassurance-seeking and the toll of years of secrecy explored.
No examination needed; hands can be checked for dermatitis; no routine investigations; functional impairment gauged by hours lost.
OCD versus generalised anxiety, depression and health anxiety considered; comorbid depression screened.
Suicidal thoughts and self-harm asked about directly; intrusive thoughts explored and distinguished from intent.
OCD named clearly with the obsession–compulsion cycle explained.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: CBT with ERP offered, plus the choice of an SSRI given at least moderate impairment (NICE CG31); self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies.
Low mood acknowledged; shame and stigma addressed; hand skin care from washing considered.
Review in 2 to 3 weeks; early review if an SSRI is started; crisis routes given.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’ve hidden it for years” and “something terrible will happen” and explored both sensitively.
Idea (unsure what it is), concern (being thought mad), expectation (to know it can be helped and to stop).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terrified that the knife thoughts mean she is dangerous and that if she tells anyone "they’ll think I’m a danger and take me away" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Miss Quinn, I’m Dr Patel. Come and sit down. What would you like to talk about today?

This is really embarrassing to say out loud. I have these thoughts I can’t get rid of, about germs, and that something terrible will happen if I don’t check things. To make the anxiety stop I wash my hands until they’re raw and check the locks over and over. I know it’s irrational, but I can’t stop. It’s taking over my life. I’ve hidden it for years.
Thank you for telling me. I can see that took courage, and you don’t need to be embarrassed here. I’d like to understand it properly. Can you tell me more about the thoughts themselves?
model.why: Validates the disclosure before gathering data

model.text: It’s mostly germs. If I touch a door handle I feel dirty, like I’ll make someone ill. And when I leave the house I get this dread that if the door isn’t locked something awful will happen, and it will be my fault.
And when that thought comes, what do you do to make it settle?
I wash, again and again, until it feels right. With the door I check the handle, go back, check again. Over and over.
Roughly how much of your day does the washing and checking take now?
model.why: Quantifies time consumed to gauge impairment

model.text: Hours. A couple of hours at least, more on a bad day. I’m late for things all the time.
How is it affecting your work, and the people around you?
Work’s suffering because I’m always late. I avoid seeing people because I can’t control things at their houses.
Are there things you now avoid altogether, or ways you get others to reassure you?
I avoid places where I can’t wash properly. Sometimes I ask people if I’ve locked up.
Some people with thoughts like these also get other unwanted thoughts that frighten them, perhaps about harm coming to others because of them. Is anything like that happening for you?
model.why: Asks sensitively about distressing intrusive thoughts

model.text: That’s the germs one, really. That I’ll be the reason someone gets ill. It feels horrible to think it.
Living with this for years sounds exhausting. How has your mood been? Have you ever had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or of harming yourself?
model.why: Screens depression and suicidal thoughts directly

model.text: I get low and fed up with myself. But no, nothing like that.
Thank you for answering that. What have you been thinking this might be?
I don’t know. I thought people would think I was mad. That’s why I never said anything.
So part of the worry has been what others might think. What were you hoping we could do today?
model.why: Names the fear of judgement; asks expectation

model.text: Just to know if it can be helped. I want to stop.
What you describe has a name: obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD. It’s common, it’s recognised, and it’s treatable. It isn’t madness and it isn’t a weakness in you.
So it’s a real thing?

Very real. It works like a cycle. An unwanted thought sends your anxiety up; washing or checking brings it down for a moment. That relief teaches your brain that the ritual was needed, so the next thought feels even more urgent. The rituals keep the cycle going.
And about the thought that you’ll make someone ill: that thought upsets you because it goes against everything you care about. It’s a symptom of OCD, not a sign of who you are.
model.why: Reassures about intrusive thoughts without dismissing

model.text: (tearful) That actually helps to hear.

The treatment with the best evidence is a talking therapy, CBT with exposure and response prevention. With a therapist you face the triggers in small steps without doing the ritual, and the anxiety fades on its own. Because this is taking hours a day, I’d also offer you the choice of an SSRI antidepressant, which helps OCD even when mood isn’t the main problem. People can have either, or both.
model.why: Offers ERP/CBT and SSRI by impairment (NICE CG31)

model.text: I’m nervous about tablets.

That’s fair. If you choose one, it’s not addictive, it can take longer to work for OCD than for depression, and sometimes it makes people feel a bit more anxious in the first couple of weeks. We’d start low and review early. You can also refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies today, and I can help with that. What would you like to do?
I’ll start with the therapy and think about the tablets.
That’s a good plan. Can you tell me in your own words what the therapy will involve?
Facing the germ stuff bit by bit without washing, so the anxiety goes down by itself.

Exactly. Let’s meet again in two to three weeks to see how the referral is going and to talk more about medication. If your mood drops, or you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999 in an emergency. You’ve done the hardest part today.

social.t: People with OCD often wait years before seeking help. Naming the condition and normalising it is part of the treatment.
Lateness and lost time can threaten her job. With her consent, a fit note with adjustments (for example flexible start times) may help while treatment starts.

legal.t: OCD that has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, entitling her to reasonable adjustments at work.
Her disclosure is confidential. Involve family or friends only with her consent.

professional.t: Clinicians sometimes misread harm-themed intrusive thoughts as risk. NICE CG31 advises seeking expert advice when genuinely uncertain rather than acting on alarm alone.
Record hours lost, functional impairment, mood, the suicide question and her answer, the treatment options discussed and her choice.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral for OCD. OCD charities offer information and peer support. Secondary care mental health services see severe or treatment-resistant OCD.

redFlags: Inability to function (not eating, not leaving home)
Psychotic features (thoughts not recognised as her own, loss of insight)
ice: Idea: unsure what it is; knows it is irrational
Concern: being judged mad; the behaviour taking over her life
Expectation: to know it can be helped, and to stop

playbook.diagnosis: “This is obsessive-compulsive disorder, OCD. Unwanted thoughts cause anxiety, and the washing and checking are the brain’s way of trying to switch that anxiety off.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The ritual brings short-term relief, which teaches your brain it was needed. That makes the next thought feel more urgent. Treatment breaks the cycle by letting the anxiety fade without the ritual.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried people would think you were mad. You’re not. This is a common, recognised condition and it responds to treatment.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the disclosure; address shame; consider work adjustments; involve others only with consent.
sharedPlan: CBT including ERP; self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies (NICE CG31)
Offer the choice of an SSRI given at least moderate impairment, dose per BNF; continue at least 12 months if it works (NICE CG31)
Secondary care referral if severe, not improving or risk rises
safetyNet: Low mood or thoughts of self-harm: contact the practice the same day, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Review in 2 to 3 weeks; within 1 week of starting an SSRI if at increased suicide risk (NICE NG222)
Worsening agitation after starting an SSRI: seek review

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards recognising a hidden condition and naming it kindly. Candidates lose marks by treating it as general anxiety, skipping the risk question, or offering vague “counselling”.

items.fail: Not naming OCD, or calling it stress or anxiety.
items.why: Naming it is therapeutic and points to the right treatment.
items.fix: Say “obsessive-compulsive disorder” and explain the cycle.

items.why: NICE CG31 matches treatment intensity to functional impairment.
items.fix: Ask how many hours a day it takes and what it stops her doing.

items.fail: Offering generic counselling rather than CBT with ERP.
items.why: ERP is the psychological treatment with the evidence for OCD (NICE CG31).
items.fix: Describe ERP in plain words and offer self-referral.

items.fail: Skipping the question about suicidal thoughts.
items.why: Depression is common alongside OCD and she has struggled alone for years.
items.fix: Ask directly and calmly, and agree a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.fail: Reacting with alarm to the thought that she might make someone ill.
items.why: It reinforces shame and misreads a symptom as intent.
items.fix: Explain that intrusive thoughts upset people because they conflict with their values.

items.fail: No review date or SSRI counselling.
items.why: SSRIs for OCD are slower to work and can cause early agitation.
items.fix: Warn about timing and side effects and book a review.

timeMap.d: Let her say it all. Thank her for telling you before the first question.
Obsession content, compulsions, hours per day, work and social impact, avoidance, reassurance-seeking, distressing intrusive thoughts.
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts. Name the fear of being thought “mad”.
OCD by name; the cycle; intrusive thoughts are symptoms, not intentions.
CBT with ERP, choice of SSRI (NICE CG31); Talking Therapies self-referral; teach-back; review in 2 to 3 weeks; crisis routes.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as generalised anxiety or tells her to try to stop; never asks how much time it takes or about mood and suicidal thoughts; offers a leaflet only; no treatment plan or review.
wordPics.pass: Recognises and names OCD, gauges impairment, screens mood and risk, offers CBT with ERP and an SSRI, and arranges follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: validates the disclosure warmly; explains the cycle in plain words; reassures about the intrusive thought that she might make others ill; matches treatment to impairment per NICE CG31; counsels on SSRI timing and early side effects; supports her choice and checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Everyone is a bit OCD about something.”
avoid.instead: “What you describe is obsessive-compulsive disorder. It’s common and treatable, and it’s clearly causing you a lot of distress.”
avoid.why: Trivialising a disabling illness deepens shame and delays help.

avoid.dont: “Just try not to wash so much.”
avoid.instead: “A therapist can help you face the triggers step by step without the ritual, so the anxiety fades on its own.”
avoid.why: Willpower advice ignores the cycle; ERP is the evidence-based way to break it (NICE CG31).

avoid.dont: “Would you ever act on that thought?” asked in an alarmed tone.
avoid.instead: “Thoughts like that are common in OCD and upset people because they go against what they care about.”
avoid.why: Treating intrusive thoughts as dangerous reinforces shame; risk is assessed calmly.

I’ll start with the therapy and think about the tablets.
That’s a good plan. Can you tell me in your own words what the therapy will involve?
Facing the germ stuff bit by bit without washing, so the anxiety goes down by itself.

Exactly. Let’s meet again in two to three weeks to see how the referral is going and to talk more about medication. If your mood drops, or you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact us the same day, or call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or 999 in an emergency. You’ve done the hardest part today.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (2005) · [2] NICE NG222 Depression in adults: treatment and management (2022, updated December 2025) · [3] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [4] BNF: selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors · [5] MHRA: SSRIs and SNRIs, use and safety
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Intrusive contamination and harm thoughts that drive hours of hand-washing and lock checking, which she knows are excessive and has hidden for years, is obsessive-compulsive disorder. The GP’s job is to name it without judgement, gauge the functional impairment (which sets the NICE CG31 treatment step), screen for depression and suicidal thoughts, reassure that intrusive thoughts are symptoms rather than intentions, and offer CBT including exposure and response prevention (ERP) and/or an SSRI with a clear review plan.

points.t: Obsessions are unwanted, recurring thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety; compulsions are repeated behaviours or mental acts done to reduce that anxiety or prevent a feared event. Hours a day of washing and checking, with preserved insight and a damaged working and social life, is OCD. Ask directly about each: people rarely volunteer the details because of shame.

Themes of harm, contamination, sex, religion or death are common in OCD and are often misread. NICE CG31 [1] advises taking expert advice where there is real uncertainty about risk from such thoughts. For most people the thoughts are unwanted and distressing precisely because they run against their values, and saying so relieves shame.

NICE CG31 [1]: mild impairment, low-intensity CBT including ERP (up to 10 therapist hours), brief individual CBT with self-help or group CBT. Moderate impairment, a choice of an SSRI or more intensive CBT including ERP (more than 10 therapist hours). Severe impairment, combined SSRI and CBT including ERP, usually with secondary care mental health involvement. Hours lost each day and impaired work and relationships suggest at least moderate impairment.

NICE CG31 [1]: SSRIs used for OCD in adults include fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline and citalopram (dose per BNF [4]). Response is often slower than in depression and higher doses may be needed. Warn about early anxiety and agitation. If effective, continue for at least 12 months, then reduce gradually. Clomipramine is considered after at least one adequate SSRI trial has failed or was not tolerated.

Depression often accompanies OCD. Ask about mood and suicidal thoughts directly. NICE NG225 [3] advises against risk tools and against labelling risk as low, medium or high: build a shared safety plan instead. NICE NG222 [2] and MHRA [5]: review within 1 week of starting an antidepressant in people aged 18 to 25 or at increased suicide risk.

NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral and delivers CBT with ERP for OCD. Refer to secondary care mental health services for severe impairment, poor response to treatment, or significant risk. Involving family or friends in the plan (with consent) can help reduce reassurance-seeking.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; validated the courage of the disclosure before questioning.
Work, social avoidance, reassurance-seeking and the toll of years of secrecy explored.
Picked up “I’ve hidden it for years” and “something terrible will happen” and explored both sensitively.
Idea (unsure what it is), concern (being thought mad), expectation (to know it can be helped and to stop).
No examination needed; hands can be checked for dermatitis; no routine investigations; functional impairment gauged by hours lost.
OCD versus generalised anxiety, depression and health anxiety considered; comorbid depression screened.
Suicidal thoughts and self-harm asked about directly; intrusive thoughts explored and distinguished from intent.
OCD named clearly with the obsession–compulsion cycle explained.
CBT with ERP offered, plus the choice of an SSRI given at least moderate impairment (NICE CG31); self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies.
Low mood acknowledged; shame and stigma addressed; hand skin care from washing considered.
Review in 2 to 3 weeks; early review if an SSRI is started; crisis routes given.

social.t: People with OCD often wait years before seeking help. Naming the condition and normalising it is part of the treatment.
Lateness and lost time can threaten her job. With her consent, a fit note with adjustments (for example flexible start times) may help while treatment starts.

legal.t: OCD that has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities can count as a disability, entitling her to reasonable adjustments at work.
Her disclosure is confidential. Involve family or friends only with her consent.

professional.t: Clinicians sometimes misread harm-themed intrusive thoughts as risk. NICE CG31 advises seeking expert advice when genuinely uncertain rather than acting on alarm alone.
Record hours lost, functional impairment, mood, the suicide question and her answer, the treatment options discussed and her choice.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral for OCD. OCD charities offer information and peer support. Secondary care mental health services see severe or treatment-resistant OCD.

redFlags: Inability to function (not eating, not leaving home)
Psychotic features (thoughts not recognised as her own, loss of insight)
ice: Idea: unsure what it is; knows it is irrational
Concern: being judged mad; the behaviour taking over her life
Expectation: to know it can be helped, and to stop

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is obsessive-compulsive disorder, OCD. Unwanted thoughts cause anxiety, and the washing and checking are the brain’s way of trying to switch that anxiety off.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The ritual brings short-term relief, which teaches your brain it was needed. That makes the next thought feel more urgent. Treatment breaks the cycle by letting the anxiety fade without the ritual.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried people would think you were mad. You’re not. This is a common, recognised condition and it responds to treatment.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the disclosure; address shame; consider work adjustments; involve others only with consent.
sharedPlan: CBT including ERP; self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies (NICE CG31)
Offer the choice of an SSRI given at least moderate impairment, dose per BNF; continue at least 12 months if it works (NICE CG31)
Secondary care referral if severe, not improving or risk rises
safetyNet: Low mood or thoughts of self-harm: contact the practice the same day, NHS 111 mental health option, or 999
Review in 2 to 3 weeks; within 1 week of starting an SSRI if at increased suicide risk (NICE NG222)
Worsening agitation after starting an SSRI: seek review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards recognising a hidden condition and naming it kindly. Candidates lose marks by treating it as general anxiety, skipping the risk question, or offering vague “counselling”.

items.fail: Not naming OCD, or calling it stress or anxiety.
items.why: Naming it is therapeutic and points to the right treatment.
items.fix: Say “obsessive-compulsive disorder” and explain the cycle.

items.why: NICE CG31 matches treatment intensity to functional impairment.
items.fix: Ask how many hours a day it takes and what it stops her doing.

items.fail: Offering generic counselling rather than CBT with ERP.
items.why: ERP is the psychological treatment with the evidence for OCD (NICE CG31).
items.fix: Describe ERP in plain words and offer self-referral.

items.fail: Skipping the question about suicidal thoughts.
items.why: Depression is common alongside OCD and she has struggled alone for years.
items.fix: Ask directly and calmly, and agree a safety plan (NICE NG225).

items.fail: Reacting with alarm to the thought that she might make someone ill.
items.why: It reinforces shame and misreads a symptom as intent.
items.fix: Explain that intrusive thoughts upset people because they conflict with their values.

items.fail: No review date or SSRI counselling.
items.why: SSRIs for OCD are slower to work and can cause early agitation.
items.fix: Warn about timing and side effects and book a review.
